events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Zara proposes Zara, Elena. As a Loyal Servant I have no private information yet, so I'm starting with myself (guaranteed Good) plus Elena on instinct for a low-risk opening mission. I'm open to revising after hearing discussion.
I'm wary of starting with Elena when we have no public evidence to assess her. I'd prefer Zara and Isha: Zara can include herself, and I know my own alignment. Zara, would you consider that revision?

Thanks for the input, Isha. I understand the instinct to pick someone who can vouch for themselves, but I'd gently push back on the idea that self-knowledge gives a teammate more value than any other player here. None of us except me can prove anything on Mission 1, so every pick besides myself is ultimately an instinct call, and Elena's is as sound as anyone's right now. What I'd like to know from you, Isha, is what specifically makes you more confident in a Zara-Isha team than Zara-Elena, beyond knowing your own role. If there's a read you're acting on, I'm open to hearing it before I decide whether to revise. As it stands, I'm inclined to keep my proposal, since I have no reason to suspect Elena and swapping now would just be trading one unknown for another.

Zara, I don't have a public read that distinguishes Elena from anyone else. My preference comes from knowing my own alignment: from my perspective, Zara and Isha has one fewer unknown than Zara and Elena. I understand you can't verify that, but I'll be more comfortable voting for a team that includes me.
I understand Zara's reasoning, but I still prefer Zara and Isha because I know my own alignment. I'll vote against Zara and Elena; that isn't a claim that I have public evidence against Elena.

Isha, I want to push back on your framing a little, because I think it could set a bad precedent for this table. Your argument for Zara-Isha is that you know your own alignment. But by that same logic every player would be entitled to insist on being included in any proposal, and every leader would end up assembling teams out of self-endorsement rather than any shared reading of the board. On Mission 1 there is no information at all, so "I know I'm good" tells the rest of us nothing new, and it certainly isn't a reason to prefer one unknown over another. Zara already explained this, and I agree with her: with no public evidence, we are choosing on instinct, and instinct doesn't have to exclude me.

I'd also note that the request here isn't really "Zara plus someone other than Elena." If Isha wants to be on the team, there is a straightforward way to do that without anyone being singled out as untrustworthy: Zara proposes Zara and Isha, and if that happens, so be it. But the current proposal is Zara and Elena, and nothing has been said that undermines it. What I don't want to see is Elena excluded from the table by a reasoning that, applied consistently, would exclude anyone and everyone. If there is an actual read on Elena, bring it, and I'll be the first to address it. There isn't one, so I'd rather we spend our remaining talk on the next team instead of relitigating this one.

One thing worth saying out loud before the vote: we will need more than two people on later missions, and every player here, Kenji and Leo included, is worth considering when the team size grows. There's no reason to narrow the pool now.

Zara, my position is that the current proposal stands and I hope you'll keep it. I'll be voting for Zara and Elena, and I'd encourage anyone who wants a different team to say plainly what evidence is driving that request rather than restating their own certainty.

Let me restate where I stand so the vote is unambiguous: I support Zara and Elena, and I don't think this proposal deserves to go down to a second rejection for the reason Isha gives.

Isha, your standard is "I know my own alignment, therefore I should be on the team." Apply that consistently and no proposal is ever safe again, because every one of us becomes an advocate for our own inclusion. You said yourself there is no public read that separates Elena from anyone else at this table, and Zara made the same point: with zero information, this choice is an instinct call, and instinct alone isn't grounds for excluding a specific player. If we're going to be picking on instinct today, let's pick on the merits of who makes a good teammate rather than on whose self-certainty is loudest. A rejection here wouldn't produce new information, it would just cost us a proposal and start a second round of the same argument with less patience in the room.

To the rest of the table, Kenji and Leo included: I don't want anyone reading my position as a case against either of you, and I want to say plainly that on the missions where the team grows to three or four, every player at this table is worth having in the pool. Elena, Kenji, Leo, Zara, Isha — we should be rotating people on rather than locking anyone out of consideration after one open mission, and I'd rather we disagree on evidence we actually have than on who gets to speak first. That's the standard I'd ask all of you to hold.

Zara, I think your instinct to include yourself and pair with someone you have no specific reason to doubt is the right one for this mission, and I'd encourage you to keep the proposal as it stands rather than revising in response to a request that isn't backed by evidence. If a revision does happen, my preference would be that it still looks like a genuine team-building choice and not like a reaction to pressure in the room. I have no hidden read on anyone here — I only know that I've heard good arguments from everyone, and that says more about this table than about any one of us. I'm voting for Zara and Elena.

I agree with the point Zara and Elena have made regarding Isha's reasoning: while it is completely understandable to trust yourself above all else, voting down proposals on Mission 1 solely because you aren't on them doesn't give Good any actionable information and quickly runs down our proposal count. Zara picking herself and testing one other person is standard. Before we move toward a vote or revision, Kenji, since you haven't spoken yet, what is your perspective on this proposal and Isha's push to swap in?

Thanks, Leo. My perspective is that the current proposal is reasonable for Mission 1. Zara has explained why she included herself and Elena, and with no public information yet, that is as defensible as any other pairing. Isha's preference for a team including herself is understandable, but it is not evidence the rest of us can act on: every player could make the same self-inclusion argument, and on Mission 1 that would not distinguish one proposal from another. I do not read Isha's push as suspicious, but I also do not see a public case that justifies swapping Elena out. At this stage I would rather keep a stable proposal than trade one unknown for another without a concrete read. I am inclined to vote for Zara and Elena.

Third and final word from me on this proposal, and I want to keep it short.

Nothing has changed since my last statement except that more of the table has now spoken, and every additional voice has landed in the same place: Zara's proposal of Zara and Elena is a reasonable instinct call, and Isha's objection rests on nothing we can act on. Kenji made the point precisely — self-inclusion is a motive, not evidence, and it is available to every player at this table equally. Leo said the same in different words. That is not a coincidence; it is the standard the rest of us are holding.

Isha, I have no hidden read on you, and I want to be clear that I am not accusing you of anything. But I am going to name the effect of the argument you are making, because I think it deserves to be named plainly before we vote: if "I know my own alignment" is sufficient grounds to reject a proposal and demand a seat, then no proposal at this table is ever safe, and every mission becomes a negotiation over who gets to advocate for themselves hardest. That is a bad operating principle for Good, and it is the one reason I would ask you to reconsider before the ballots are cast. Zara and Elena is not a case against you — it is a case for not making you a case against anyone.

Zara, my position has not moved: keep the proposal exactly as it stands, do not revise in response to a request that carries no read, and let it go to a vote. A revision here would not be team-building; it would be a reaction to pressure, and it would cost us one of our five proposals on a mission where we have no information to spend.

Kenji, Leo — if you are inclined as you have indicated, the useful thing now is to make sure the vote settles the argument rather than reopening it. I would rather this team fail or succeed on the mission result and leave us with a clear board to read next than spend another round of talk on the same two-person dispute.

One last thing, for the missions ahead. Team sizes grow to three and then four, and every player here — Zara, Isha, Kenji, Leo, and me — should be treated as a serious candidate on those teams. Nobody should read today's vote as settling who matters later. I am voting for Zara and Elena, and I recommend the same.

This discussion has run its course, and I want to bring it to a close. I'm keeping my proposal of Zara and Elena exactly as it stands.

The table has heard the same argument from both sides now, several times over. Isha's case is that she knows her own alignment and would feel more comfortable on a team that includes her. I understand the feeling, and I don't think it makes Isha suspicious — but as Kenji, Leo, and Elena have all said, self-knowledge is available to every player equally and cannot function as a criterion for who gets a seat. If I accepted it here, the next leader would face the same demand, and every proposal from now on would be shaped by whoever advocates hardest for inclusion rather than by any read on the board. That's a standard Good can't afford.

On my end, nothing has changed. I am Loyal, I know I'm Good, and I have no reason to doubt Elena. On a two-person Mission 1 with no public information, my pick is an instinct call, and I'm comfortable standing behind it. Swapping Elena for Isha would trade one unknown for another at the cost of looking like I cave to pressure rather than reason, and I don't think that sets a good precedent for how leadership works at this table.

I do want to say two things before we vote. First, Isha: this is nothing personal, and I hope you'll vote your honest read — but a vote against this team should be understood as what it is, a preference, not evidence against Elena or anyone else. Second, to Kenji and Leo and everyone else: today's disagreement shouldn't lock anyone out of future teams. Missions grow to three and four players, and every person here will be under serious consideration. What we should all be watching after the vote is simply the mission result and, later, how people behave when they hold information. That's where real reads come from, not from opening-day advocacy.

So my position is final: the team is Zara and Elena, it goes to a vote as proposed, and I'm asking the table to approve it. If it fails on the mission, we'll learn something real; if it succeeds, we've banked a win at zero information cost, which is exactly what Mission 1 is for. Either outcome gives us more than another round of this argument would. Let's vote.

Zara confirms Zara, Elena. The discussion is settled: no one has produced a read against Elena, and Isha's preference is self-inclusion, not evidence. Swapping one unknown for another would only reward pressure. I'm keeping Zara and Elena and sending it to a vote.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Leo proposes Leo, Kenji, Isha. Mission 1 failed with one fail card, proving that at least one of Zara or Elena is Evil. As a Loyal Servant, I know I am Good, and Isha is notable for being the sole player to vote against that failed proposal. Starting with the three players off Mission 1 (Leo, Kenji, Isha) provides our cleanest baseline and forces Zara and Elena to state their reads on each other.

I don't think being off Mission 1 clears Kenji. Kenji supported Zara and Elena without much independent scrutiny, and the failed mission gives us reason to reconsider that approval. I was also struck by how strongly Elena pushed the team and framed opposition as bad for Good.

I'd prefer Leo, Isha, Zara: it includes me and avoids both Elena and Kenji. Zara is not cleared by the result, but I find Elena's forceful defense more concerning than Zara's initial instinct pick.

Leo, would you consider replacing Kenji with Zara?

Isha, I understand your concern about Kenji's vote on Mission 1, but swapping Kenji for Zara right now carries significant risk. Mission 1 failed, meaning at least one of Zara or Elena is Evil. If we substitute Zara in without hearing from her or Elena first, we risk putting the very player who threw that fail right back onto a crucial 3-person mission. Leaving both of them off was specifically meant to force them to address the table, because one of them definitely betrayed Good. I do agree with you that Elena's aggressive defense of the Mission 1 pairing looks terrible in hindsight given the outcome. Before I consider any revisions to this proposal, I want to hear directly from Zara. Zara, you selected Elena and confirmed the team that resulted in a fail. Do you believe Elena submitted the fail card, and how do you evaluate Isha's proposal to swap you onto this team in place of Kenji?

Leo, you asked me directly, so here is my answer as plainly as I can put it. I am Good. I played a Success card on Mission 1. The mission failed with exactly one Fail card, and I was one of only two people on that mission. That means, with certainty from my perspective, Elena submitted the Fail card. I understand that from the table's point of view this is just my word against the board, but it is the strongest information anyone at this table holds right now: one of Zara or Elena is Evil, I know I am not, so I am telling you Elena is. Every read I offer from here on flows from that. On Isha's suggestion to swap me onto this team in place of Kenji: I would decline it, and I want to be clear about why, because it is not false modesty. Putting me on the team adds nothing — I was always going to play Success. The real question for this mission is whether it contains the Evil player we have now partially identified, and your proposal of Leo, Kenji, Isha already keeps Elena off, which is exactly where she should stay. Kenji voted to approve the Mission 1 team, but voters do not hold mission cards, so that approval tells us nothing about his cards. I have no read against Kenji or Isha beyond what anyone can observe. That said, I will flag one pattern honestly, because I would want it flagged if I were in your seats. Isha voted against the Mission 1 team while insisting on her own inclusion, and is now on this team after advocating for a revision that includes her. I do not think that is damning — her stated reasoning was self-knowledge, which is available to everyone — but if this mission fails, Isha's advocacy for her own seat is the first place I would look, the same way you are all now looking at me and Elena. I would rather say that now than seem to be shielding anyone later. So my recommendation to you, Leo, is to keep Leo, Kenji, Isha exactly as proposed. It excludes the player I believe is Evil, it gives the table a clean baseline, and it does not reward pressure-based revision — which, as I said before the last vote, is a precedent this table should not set. If you feel you must include me, I will play Success and I will not fail you, but I genuinely think your current three is the better team for extracting information: if it succeeds, my accusation against Elena sharpens considerably, because the Evil player would have been off the mission. Elena, I am going to put the question to you straight, the same way Leo put it to me: are you Evil, and did you play the Fail card on Mission 1? If you are Good, say so and tell the table why you believe the Fail card came from

I still prefer Leo, Isha, Zara. Elena's repeated, forceful defense of the first team looks worse to me than Zara's initial selection, and Kenji's approval adds to my concern about him. Neither read is proof, but leaving Zara off only guarantees we exclude at least one Evil player; it doesn't clear the proposed three. I will vote against Leo, Kenji, Isha.

Leo's proposal is the right shape for Mission 2. Mission 1 failed with one Fail card, so from the public board at least one of Zara or Elena is Evil. I will not pretend Zara's statement that Elena is the culprit settles it; from everyone else's seat that is Zara's word against Elena's, and Zara has an obvious interest in directing suspicion away from herself. That is not proof against Zara, but it is a reason not to treat her accusation as established. The cleanest next test is a team that includes neither Mission 1 participant. Leo, Kenji, Isha does that. I know my own alignment, and I have no private read against Leo; I would rather approve this baseline than swap in Zara on the strength of an unverifiable claim. Isha's earlier preference for including herself was not evidence, but she is on this team now, and the mission result will tell us more than another round of self-advocacy. I intend to vote approve.

I'm still voting against Leo, Kenji, Isha. Excluding Zara and Elena guarantees only that at least one Evil player is left off; it does not make the proposed team safe. Kenji's support for the failed team and his quick endorsement of this one concern me. I'd rather take the risk on Zara, whose response and initial conduct I find more credible than Elena's repeated defense of the failed pairing. Leo, I urge you to reconsider Leo, Isha, Zara.

Zara, you've asked me directly whether I'm Evil, so let me answer plainly: I am a Loyal Servant, and my Mission 1 card was Success. I have no hidden read on anyone at this table — not on Kenji, not on Isha, not on you.

Zara, I want to point at the one part of your statement that actually needs scrutiny, because it's the part you skipped. On Mission 1 you chose Elena before you had any information about her, and you confirmed that team when asked to revise it. If Elena turned out to be the source of the Fail card, then the team that failed was assembled by you. I'm not accusing you of anything — you may genuinely be Good — but notice what your accusation does: it takes a 50/50 board and lands entirely on the person who had no way to defend herself, while the person who put her on the team and had every opportunity to swap her out is treated as the source of truth. If your read is right, then Mission 1 failed because of a selection you made and defended. If your read is wrong, then you've just told the table that your accusation against me was an inference from a failed mission rather than from anything you observed. Only one of those two things is Good play, and I don't think the table should treat either of them as settled.

Isha, I notice your position moved. On Mission 1 you wanted a seat on the team and called yourself uncertain about me. Now you're certain I'm Evil and you want Zara on instead — but Zara is the one player who has told us plainly that her own Mission 1 card was Success, and she had no reason to make that claim unless she believed it. Kenji has been consistent throughout and has no stake in either of these pairings. Zara is the only name on this board whose interest points toward my exclusion, and that's a fact worth naming out loud.

On the proposal itself: Leo, Kenji, Isha is a reasonable Mission 2 team. It puts both of us who went on Mission 1 off the board, so whatever happens here gives us real information about the Mission 1 fail, and it doesn't reward the pattern of demanding a seat and then calling the result of your own exclusion suspicious. If this mission succeeds, we'll have a strong signal that the Evil player is among Zara and me; if it fails, we'll have learned that a third player is failing us, which is information nobody in this room wants but everyone needs.

Zara, if you're confident enough to call me Evil, then be confident enough to say what you think I'm doing on Mission 2 — and if the answer is 'nothing, because I'm not on the team,' then consider what that says about who actually benefits from this team's composition.

I'm voting to approve Leo, Kenji, Isha.

I stay with Leo, Kenji, Isha, and I want to be precise about why Isha's revision is the riskier of the two proposals.

Zara's Mission 2 case rests on a claim nobody at this table can check. Only team members hold mission cards. Zara's account of her own Mission 1 card, and her accusation against me, are both self-reports from an interested party, and I notice the shape of it: the claim lands with precision on the one person who could not answer it in a way anyone here could verify. If Zara were Evil, everything she has said — the instinct pick, the confident denial, the finger pointed at a teammate — would look exactly as it does now. That is precisely why I don't want Zara added to this team on the strength of her own word. Put her on, and a Mission 2 failure could always be attributed to the player asking to be there, which destroys the only clean read this mission can produce.

Kenji's Mission 1 approval is likewise not evidence. He held no card that could fail that mission, and he explained his reasoning at the time; his position has been consistent since. Isha's read on me is the opposite of evidence — it is an impression built from how forcefully I argued, and I would rather the table weigh my actions than my tone. I said I was Loyal and played Success on Mission 1; Isha is welcome to distrust that, but distrust is not a read.

What Leo, Kenji, Isha does is take both Mission 1 players off the board, so the result here gives us real information about the fail instead of another round of argument about it. If this mission succeeds, the Evil player lies among Zara and me and we know to look at us. If it fails, we have learned a third player failed us, and every person here deserves equal scrutiny for that — nobody should read my pushback as a case against Zara or against anyone on this team.

One forward-looking note, offered in the same spirit: Zara and I have now both been on a failed mission, so until this table has information about that pair, neither of us should be the obvious choice for the next team either. Clean tests give clean reads.

I vote to approve Leo, Kenji, Isha.

Isha, I hear your concerns, but I am going to keep my proposal as Leo, Kenji, Isha. Kenji voting to approve Mission 1 is not evidence of evil alignment—four of us voted to approve that team, including myself. If voting to approve an instinct-based Mission 1 proposal makes someone suspect, then by that metric I would be suspect too, which I know is false. Furthermore, Zara herself explicitly declined the swap and recommended keeping Leo, Kenji, Isha to maintain a clean baseline. Swapping Zara in brings someone from a confirmed failed mission straight onto Mission 2 when we have no way to verify whether she or Elena threw the Fail card. Keeping both Zara and Elena off gives us the purest possible read: if this mission passes, we heavily narrow our focus to Zara and Elena; if it fails, we know another evil player is among Kenji and Isha. I am sticking with Leo, Kenji, Isha.

Third and final word from me, and this time I want to attack the weakest joint in Isha's case rather than restate my own position.

Isha's revision is Leo, Isha, Zara. It removes Kenji and adds Zara. So let me name what that swap actually does at the table. Kenji approved Mission 1 — as did Zara, as did Leo, and as did I. If approving the failed team is now evidence of Evil, then four of the five people in this room are suspect and we have no proposal left to make. Kenji is being removed from a team not because anyone read him, but because he declined to swap in a player on the strength of that player's own account of herself. That is a decision about Zara's confidence in herself, dressed up as a read on Kenji.

And the read on me that justifies all of it comes from Zara's statement that she played Success on Mission 1 and therefore I must have played Fail. Nobody here can verify any part of that. It is exactly the shape of claim I would expect from someone who needs to redirect attention away from the team she assembled and defended on Mission 1, and I notice that this same person is now the only name Isha wants to add to the board. Zara, I said before that your accusation lands entirely on the one person who had no way to answer it, and nothing in this mission has changed that. I am not accusing you of being Evil — I don't know that, and I have no hidden read on you or on anyone else. But I am pointing out that Isha is offering to trade a player with no read against him for a player with no read against me, and the only thing connecting the two is how forcefully I argued on Mission 1. Tone is not a card.

One point in Isha's favor that I'll grant: she has been consistent in stating her position, and consistency is worth something. But Leo, Kenji, Isha is also a genuinely clean test. If it passes, we have learned something real and hard about the Mission 1 pair. If it fails, we have learned that the failure is not confined to Zara and me, and every player here deserves to be examined equally — including, I want to say plainly, me, and including Kenji.

I vote to approve Leo, Kenji, Isha. Please take the mission result as the read rather than another round of who sounds more certain about whom.
Leo confirms Leo, Kenji, Isha. Keeping both players from the failed Mission 1 off the team provides the cleanest baseline and most informative result. I am confirming Leo, Kenji, and Isha.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).
Isha proposes Isha, Zara. I trust Zara more than Elena after Mission 1, and I know my own alignment. This pairing gives us the best chance to stop a third failure.

Table, we are at match point. Evil has two mission wins; one more fail card and Evil wins the game right here on Mission 3.

Let us look at the undeniable deductions from the board:
In a 5-player game, there are exactly 2 Evil players. 
Mission 1 failed, meaning exactly one of Zara or Elena is Evil.
Mission 2 also failed with 1 fail card. I was on that mission, I am a Loyal Servant, and I played a Success card. That means exactly one of Kenji or Isha is Evil.
Between Kenji and Isha, Kenji is by far the most suspect: Kenji approved Mission 1, approved Mission 2, and sat on Mission 2 when it failed, whereas Isha consistently voted against both failed teams.

However, look at the proposal currently on the floor: Isha and Zara. 
This team completely excludes me. By picking one person from {Kenji, Isha} and one person from {Zara, Elena}, you are gambling on two separate 50/50s simultaneously. If Zara is the Evil player from Mission 1, the mission fails and Evil wins. If Isha is Evil, the mission fails and Evil wins. Both of them have to be Good for that team to pass.

I know 100% that I am Good. Putting me on this 2-person team cuts the risk in half because it guarantees one slot is Good, meaning we only have to get one read right instead of two.

Isha, given that Evil needs only one more fail to win the game, will you revise this proposal to include me instead of taking an unnecessary gamble on both yourself and Zara?

Leo, I understand why you want a seat: from your perspective, you know you're Good. From mine, I know I'm Good, and I trust Zara more than Elena on the first mission. I also think Kenji's consistent support for both failed teams is concerning. Your proposed change would require me to trust two other players rather than one.

I'm keeping Isha and Zara. We cannot afford another failed mission, and this is the pairing I trust most.

At match point, this is the wrong team. Isha and Zara is a double gamble: Zara is one of the two unresolved Mission 1 participants, and Isha is one of the players left in the Mission 2 failure. From the public board, those are the two unresolved failure pairs, and this proposal puts one name from each on the same team. If either unresolved suspicion is correct, Evil gets its third fail immediately. Isha's voting against the earlier teams does not erase that she was on the Mission 2 team that failed, and now she is using leadership to put herself back on the board. I am not saying Zara is proven Evil, but at match point we should not combine two unverified names and call it caution. The safer shape is a team anchored by Leo's public reasoning and not built around the leader's own seat. I will vote against Isha and Zara and ask others to do the same.

Table, Kenji's framing is correct and I want to build on it rather than argue against it, because it points at a better team than the one on the floor. Here is the board, stated plainly. Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card, and only Zara and Elena were on it, so exactly one of the two of us is Evil. Mission 2 failed with exactly one Fail card on a completely disjoint team, Leo, Kenji and Isha, so exactly one of those three is Evil. There is no third Evil player to hide elsewhere; two are on the board and they are sitting in these two buckets. Every two-person team therefore picks one name from {Zara, Elena} and one name from {Leo, Kenji, Isha}, and Isha's proposal puts two unresolved names on the same team at once. Two coin flips, not one. At match point, where one Fail ends the game, that is the shape I want to avoid if there is any better shape available, and there is. The better shape is a known-good anchor plus one 50/50. Leo, you made exactly this argument yourself and you are right about it: nobody at this table has a read against you, and your votes on Mission 1 and Mission 2 were votes alongside a majority, which is not evidence of anything. So anchor on Leo and take one name from the first bucket. I am offering myself, Elena, and I am doing so plainly rather than as a manoeuvre: I am Loyal, my Mission 1 card was Success, and I have no hidden read on Zara, on Kenji, on Leo or on Isha. I am not asking the table to trust me. I am asking it to take the risk with me, because the alternative is taking two risks at once. Why me and not Zara? Not because I have read against her, because I do not. It is the information value. If this team fails, the failure is attributed to one of us and the Mission 1 pair is resolved on the spot, and the table will know to look hard at Kenji and Isha for the second Evil. If it passes, we have cleared that pair outright. Either outcome is a hard read. Isha plus Zara gives us the same information only after a coin flip has already cost us a mission. Isha, will you take me in place of Zara, keeping your own seat, or if you prefer Leo's framing, would you let Leo and me take it? You have a revision available and I would rather you used it than send two unresolved names into the last mission we can afford. Kenji, I take no read against you and I ask that you take none against me beyond what the board shows. Leo, you wanted this seat and you argued for it; I am telling you that if you take it with me, I am not going to let you down, because the only

I am voting against Isha and Zara. At match point, the public board has two unresolved failure buckets: one of Zara or Elena from Mission 1, and one of Leo, Kenji, or Isha from Mission 2. Isha's proposal puts Zara and Isha together — one unresolved name from each bucket. That is not a safe team; it is two unresolved bets combined in the same proposal. Isha says she trusts Zara and knows her own alignment, but self-knowledge is not public evidence, and she made the same self-inclusion argument on Mission 1. After Mission 2 failed with Isha on the team, leadership should not now put Isha back on the board without a cleaner public reason. I do not have a read against Zara, but she remains inside the Mission 1 pair, and pairing her with another unresolved Mission 2 name is exactly the double gamble we cannot afford. The safer shape is an anchor plus one unresolved name, not two unresolved names at once. Leo, you made this argument directly to Isha and asked her to revise; she refused. Will you join me in voting down Isha and Zara so the next proposal can use a cleaner shape? I will reject this team.

Kenji, you just asked me to join you in voting down Isha and Zara, but your plea has made the entire game crystal clear.

Consider the situation: Evil sits at match point with two mission victories. If either Isha or Zara were Evil, Evil would already have a game-winning team right here on Mission 3. A single Fail card ends the game on the spot. If Isha were Evil, or if Zara were Evil, why on earth would you, Kenji, and Elena both spend every speaking turn desperately campaigning to reject this proposal? Evil would never fight tooth and nail to dismantle their own immediate win condition.

The only rational explanation for why both of you are frantic to shoot down Isha and Zara is that neither of you is on it. Without an Evil player on the mission, you cannot fail it, and Good takes a win.

Now look back at the history: on Mission 1, both Kenji and Elena approved, and the mission failed. On Mission 2, both Kenji and Elena approved, and the mission failed. Now, on Mission 3, the moment a proposal excludes both of you, Elena volunteers to take a seat with me, and Kenji begs me to vote reject so we can assemble a 'safer' team. 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
